title: System Design Practice
description: Use small examples to practise system design. Work out demand, spot risky choices, and choose a useful next step. Read the explanation after each answer.

exercises.question: Which line gives a goal we can measure?
options: Make the service amazing
95 of 100 searches finish within 2 seconds
Use as many servers as possible
exercises.explanation: A measured goal says what to count and the limit to check. We can time the searches and count how many finish within 2 seconds.

exercises.question: Which is a rule about correct data?
options: Use a blue page header
One copy cannot have two active loans
Buy two more computers
exercises.explanation: The loan rule protects a real library fact. Colors and equipment choices do not replace the need to keep that fact correct.

exercises.question: The reply to a request is called a ___.
exercises.explanation: A response is the reply to a request. It may contain useful data, an empty result, or information about a problem.

exercises.question: A class makes 240 searches in 120 seconds. Its average rate is ___ searches per second.
exercises.explanation: Divide searches by seconds: 240 divided by 120 is 2 searches per second. This rate is an average for that period.

exercises.question: Which measurement describes throughput?
options: 200 ms for one search
40 completed searches in 2 seconds
One search that timed out
exercises.explanation: Throughput counts completed work over time. Forty completed searches in 2 seconds means an average throughput of 20 searches per second.

exercises.question: Why does the search API limit each page to at most 20 records?
options: To keep the amount of work and reply size bounded
To guarantee that no request can fail
To remove the need to check input
exercises.explanation: A page limit bounds each reply and limits work per request. It does not remove failures or replace input checks.

exercises.question: What does bookId=17 in copy 203 mean?
options: The copy is on shelf 17
The copy belongs to book record 17
The copy has been borrowed 17 times
exercises.explanation: bookId is the link from a physical copy to the shared book record. The shelf and borrowing history are different facts.

exercises.question: What is the best starting point for choosing a database?
options: The questions and update rules the app needs
Which product has the brightest logo
The idea that all NoSQL databases behave the same
exercises.explanation: The needed reads, writes, and correctness rules help you compare real database features. A family name alone does not answer those questions.

exercises.question: What extra work can a title index cause when a title changes?
options: The index may need an update
The database must delete every book
Every reader must change their browser
exercises.explanation: The index stores information about title values. When a stored title changes, the database may need to update that extra structure too.

exercises.question: The conditional UPDATE changes zero rows. What should this request do?
options: Create a second loan anyway
Report that this attempt did not claim the copy
Assume the earlier check is still true
exercises.explanation: Zero changed rows means the condition did not hold. This request did not claim the copy, so it must not create a loan as if it had.

exercises.question: Three app servers can do 120 searches/s, but the shared database can do 90. What is this model's whole-service limit?
options: 40 searches/s
90 searches/s
120 searches/s
exercises.explanation: The whole request must pass through both parts. The smaller capacity, 90 searches per second, sets this model's limit.

exercises.question: Which server receives the third request in this small round-robin model?
options: A
B
C
exercises.explanation: The remainder of 2 divided by 2 is 0. Index 0 holds A, so the third request returns to A.

exercises.question: The main title changes at time 6, but its cache expires at time 10. What can a read at time 7 return?
options: Only the new title
The old cached title
No title can ever be returned
exercises.explanation: The cache can reuse the old value until expiry unless a working refresh or invalidation rule changes it sooner.

exercises.question: Which item is the clearest choice for a shared public CDN cache?
options: A public book-cover image
A learner's private borrowing history
A staff password-reset response
exercises.explanation: Every reader may receive the same public cover. The other responses need private handling and must not be shared publicly.

exercises.question: An accidental delete is copied to every replica. Which extra plan can help recover the earlier record?
options: More reads from the same replicas
A tested backup or point-in-time recovery plan
Changing the page color
exercises.explanation: A backup or retained history can recover an earlier state. Replicas alone may all contain the same bad change.

exercises.question: With shard = bookId % 3, book 14 belongs to shard ___.
exercises.explanation: 14 divided by 3 leaves a remainder of 2. The three shard numbers are 0, 1, and 2.

exercises.question: A replica is behind after a successful title edit. Which statement fits eventual consistency?
options: Every read must already show the edit
A read may show the old title while the replica catches up
The replicas can never agree again
exercises.explanation: Eventual consistency allows a delay. Copies converge once updates stop and communication and repair can complete; no fixed delay is implied.

exercises.question: Five jobs arrive and three finish each round. Starting from zero, how many wait after three rounds?
exercises.explanation: The backlog grows by 2 each round. After three rounds it contains 6 jobs.

exercises.question: A reservation succeeds but its reply is lost. Which request should a safe retry use?
options: The same action details and the same idempotency key
A new key for every attempt
A different book ID to avoid waiting
exercises.explanation: The same key lets the service recognize the same intended action and return its recorded result under its idempotency rules.

exercises.question: What does this circuit breaker do in its open state?
options: Send every request immediately
Reject calls quickly until its recovery test is allowed
Erase the database
exercises.explanation: The open state pauses calls to the dependency. After a cooldown, a limited half-open probe tests recovery.

exercises.question: The waiting tray is full. Which action applies backpressure?
options: Add work forever
Ask the sender to slow down
Tell every request it succeeded
exercises.explanation: Backpressure tells the sender that the next part cannot accept more work yet. A bounded tray prevents endless waiting and memory growth.

exercises.question: The last good backup is at 12:00 and data is damaged at 12:40. How much recent work may be missing?
options: 15 minutes
40 minutes
100 minutes
exercises.explanation: There are 40 minutes between the last saved copy and the damage. Restore duration is a different measurement.

exercises.question: A dashboard shows 2 errors among 40 requests. What is the error rate?
options: 2 percent
5 percent
20 percent
exercises.explanation: Divide 2 by 40 and multiply by 100. The result is 5 percent. The number of requests matters when comparing error counts.

exercises.question: A reader changes a record ID in a request. Which check prevents them from seeing another reader's loans?
options: Hide the browser button
Check permission for the requested records in the service
Use a longer page title
exercises.explanation: The service must check authorization for the exact records being requested. Browser controls alone cannot enforce access rules.

exercises.question: Which is the strongest reason to split the reminder module into a separate service?
options: A bigger diagram looks better
Measured reminder load needs independent capacity and the team can operate the split
Every small app needs ten services
exercises.explanation: A split should solve a real need and have a team ready for its extra work. Clear modules are useful even when the app stays in one deployment.

exercises.question: Two readers try to borrow the same available copy at the same time. What must the design protect?
options: Each request must get a success message
Only one current loan may be saved for that copy
The cached page must always win
exercises.explanation: The database must enforce the loan rule while saving related changes together. One request succeeds; the other gets a clear refusal.

exercises.question: A code generator produces a code already stored for another destination. What is the safe next step?
options: Overwrite the existing destination
Try a new code after the unique insert fails
Send visitors to a random site
exercises.explanation: The stored mapping belongs to the earlier link. A unique database rule prevents replacement, and bounded retries can choose a new code.

exercises.question: A message was saved but the sender lost the reply. How should the sender retry?
options: Use the same client message ID for the same text
Generate a new ID every millisecond
Delete the whole conversation
exercises.explanation: Keeping the same ID lets the service find the saved outcome and avoid saving the same send twice.

exercises.question: One author gains a million followers. Which cost grows sharply with building feeds on write?
options: The number of feed entries added for one post
The number of letters in the author's name
The size of every request ID
exercises.explanation: Fan-out may create one entry for each follower. A popular account can make one small post turn into a large amount of work.

exercises.question: Upload bytes arrived, but the required checks have not finished. Which state is correct?
options: Ready for every reader
Checking
Deleted from every backup
exercises.explanation: Uploaded and ready are different states. The file remains unavailable until the required checks pass on the version that will be served.
